issue: Applying for a mortgage or refinancing an existing mortgage
narrative: My boyfriend and I applied with this lender in XXXX of XXXX. He told us at the time of approval that he could get us approved for up to {$400000.00} with the possibility of some debts being paid down. He then recommended a realtor that he was worked with that has experience with XXXX loans which is what we got approved for. XXXX, the lender, already assured us that we had been approved to purchase a home and that we were okay to put in offers. We put in offers on a few homes and each time the realtor would ask the lender to draft up an approval letter based off of the amount that we were putting the offer in on the home. Our process started off okay but then it went completely downhill. My boyfriend and I finally found a home that we both liked and were wanting to move forward with and that was XX/XX/XXXX of XXXX. Prior to this, we already had an issue with the lender not disclosing issues with our credit. Before putting down our offer we had asked the lender to give us our cash to close amount that way we made sure we were on track. The lender gave us the information but the amount he gave us was about {$10000.00} more than we were expecting. When I inquired and asked why, he said that due to my boyfriend having such a low XXXX XXXX, his company was saying it is MANDATORY for us to buy down the rate. I told him I've never heard of anything being required but optional for us if we want to pay a higher mortgage then that should be our choice. At this time we were also looking into the option of another lender, so I gave her a call and told her what XXXX was saying in regards to the rate. She assured me that she's never heard of that being a requirement and she ran numbers on their end and the numbers she had given us were completely different including the interest rate and down payment required. My boyfriend and I were highly upset and expressed this issue with our realtor and told him we do not want to move forward with this lender being that he was already dishonest and tried to slip in extra monies without disclosing it with us prior. My realtor told us that we had nothing to worry about and that he would talk with the lender and get this resolved. The lender then reached out to us asking for a copy of the numbers we had received from the other lender. Moments later, we received a text from XXXX saying that " all of a sudden '' he had no problem matching the other lenders offer. My boyfriend and I still weren't too excited, but our realtor assured us that we would be fine and to move forward. We finally got our offer accepted on the home we wanted on XX/XX/XXXX which included a {$10000.00} non-refundable deposit that was suggested by our realtor to make the offer look strong and also approved by the lender. After the offer had been accepted and we were moving forward, the lender decided to let us know that there may be an issue with my boyfriends overtime and he is not sure he will be able to get the loan approved and the only way to get this resolved is by having his HR send a letter to him stating that overtime is mandatory. Our realtor told us to not give the deposit until this issue was resolved to make sure this deal would move forward. After about 2 days of going back and forth with my boyfriends HR we were told that our lender received the necessary letter and that he would double check with his underwriting team to make sure this will not push the loan out of approval for the home. We asked for a copy for a copy of letter at least twice which we never received although we were told we were. The next communications that we received were from our realtor letting us know that we were good to send in the money for the deposit, so we assumed that everything had been resolved. For the next XXXX weeks we were finalizing paperwork and any documentation that the lender needed from us. We were set to close on XX/XX/XXXX. XX/XX/XXXX is when the lender told us that his underwriter is not able to approve our loan based off of the letter that was received from my boyfriends HR, because it stated that although overtime is mandatory it can not be guaranteed in the future. XXXX told us that the only way we can move forward is by having a co-signer. My boyfriend and I were not too fond of this idea at first but ended up deciding to see if we could ask my parents for help. This ended up not being possible being the fact that they haven't had to file taxes for a few years. The lender asked us if we could ask any other family members and then we can refinance in 6 months and have them removed, and I said none of my family members have the credit or ability to have this added to them financially. He then asked my boyfriend and I if we could use his sister. We both said no, because she herself had just bough her first home XX/XX/XXXX and we don't want to add a {$350000.00} loan onto her on top of that. XXXX, the lender, told us that it would be fine and it won't affect her at all. We told him no, because her credit and financials were not in the place for this. At this point our realtor told us we were at risk of losing our {$10000.00} if we didn't figure out a way to get this done. Again, the lender reached out to me personally and asked me to talk to my sister in law which I reminded him that we already expressed to him why we can't do that. He then reached out to my boyfriend personally and asked him to talk to his sister in which my boyfriend replied and reminded him that we already said that we would not do that. All of this had pushed us into XXXX at this point. The lender finally said that he thinks he can get us approved but he needs an updated letter. I raised the concern that isn't that altering a legal document since HR already submitted paperwork, so If you get a new letter based off of a statement that you need it to say, I am worried underwriting would flag our whole account. He said no it's okay and wouldn't hurt us. The lender asked if my boyfriend could get a letter from his direct supervisor stating overtime was mandatory. My boyfriend said he would try. He reached out to his direct supervisor but in turn the supervisor said that if XXXX already submitted paperwork, that he can't send anything discounting that because it would be against company policy since XXXX has the final say. XXXX and the realtor then again asked my boyfriend to reach out to his HR. At this point we are completely frustrated and upset and wondering why all of this was not taken care of before we put in an offer and had it accepted. We are trying to work with our realtor to see how we can get our deposit back in which we are told our only option is to move forward and purchase or give up the money. After all of this time the realtor still hasn't handed over the check, it was in his possession. The realtor and the lender took it upon themselves to reach out to my boyfriends HR even after he had asked them not to and they ended up getting a completely different letter on XX/XX/XXXX. XXXX said he would submit that to underwriting which was XX/XX/XXXX and was hoping to have an answer. On XX/XX/XXXX ( our original closing date ) he said we were being given a second chance and asked for some more information which I sent to them that day. XX/XX/XXXX is when underwriting finally approved our file. My boyfriend and I sent a proposal for different terms on XXXX XXXX let the lender and realtor know that since the contract stated our close date was supposed to be XX/XX/XXXX and we didn't meet that date our contract was voided per the language of the contract and that we can only move forward with the loan with new terms. The realtor didn't respond to us until XX/XX/XXXX. I had been traveling and dealing with legal issues at the time so I wasn't able to send a response until XX/XX/XXXX and the realtor was asking the lender to close the file. XX/XX/XXXX we talked to the realtor an explored our options, we told the realtor we can not close until XX/XX/XXXX to move forward due to emergency expenses and that the money would be ready by then. The realtor told us that the seller is not able to close in XXXX and that the seller will have to be the one to terminate the contract and that we will still not be able to get our money back. We said okay we have no other choice then. The realtor told the lender it was our choice to terminate but we said that we are not able to agree to terms with seller and so the deal can't move froward. XX/XX/XXXX we received and email requesting documentation to move forward and close the loan. The realtor responded and said the file will be not be moving forward. XX/XX/XXXX I checked our online portal and saw that we had been transferred to a new lender, XXXX. XX/XX/XXXX the lender reaches out to me asking to sign the realtors termination letter on behalf of the realtor. I called the Lender 's company and spoke to XXXX XXXX, Compliance Senior Vice President, on XX/XX/XXXX letting her know what happened and she apologized and said that is not how the company is run, she said that the only way to move forward with an investigation is to have the loan and file closed out because right now we have an open loan just sitting there not doing anything and I agreed. She asked me to send her documentation which I did. A few weeks later we received a letter from the XXXX company stating that the fault was ours for not sending documentation when it was being requested of us and that we prolonged things moving forward. This was the last communications that we had.

Without proof of lawful assignment, Sunrise Credit Services has no permissible purpose to report this account. Demand for Resolution I hereby demand that Sunrise Credit Services : Immediately delete this tradeline from all consumer reporting agencies, including XXXX, XXXX, and XXXX. The primary statute in Illinois requiring licensing in the area of debt collection is the Illinois Collection Agency Act. ( 225 ILCS 425 et seq ). Under the Act, anyone acting as a collection agency must obtain a collection agency license. An entity is considered to be acting as a collection agency when, among other things, it engages in the collection of debts for others or buys accounts, bills or other indebtedness and engages in collecting the same ( 225 ILCS 425/3 ). Debt collection is defined as any act or practice in connection with only consumer debts 225 ILCS 425/2 ). Even out-of-state debt buyers must be licensed, if they buy and sue on consumer accounts in Illinois ( XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXXXXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX ) ). To obtain the collection agency license, a {$750.00} fee must accompany the application, along with a bond for {$25000.00}. The applicant must also provide an employment history, financial statement, employee identity listing and trust account financial report. Im a victim of identity theft, I have no knowledge of these accounts nor any involvement with SPRING OAKS CAPITAL LLC. I disputed these 2 fraudulent accounts with the credit bureaus, attached a ftc identity theft report, and police report showing that Im a victim of identity theft. The credit bureaus informed me that they sent the dispute with the documents to this company. I have neither engaged in business transactions with them nor entered into any agreements. Hence, it is unjustified for them to report fraudulent accounts that I have no knowledge of. This situation infringes upon my rights as a consumer, as outlined by the FCRA and FDCPA. Im attaching my current ftc identity theft report and police report to this complaint which show evidence that I'm a victim of identity theft. I filed a complaint with the bbb and my ftc identity theft report was NOT ACKNOWLEDGED. This company is still saying that these 2 fraudulent accounts are VALID and are trying to make me liable for these fraud accounts! When a ftc identity theft report or police report is sent to a company from a consumer it validates the identity theft that the consumer is reporting. An FTC Identity Theft Report is a document generated by the Federal Trade Commission ( FTC ) that allows victims of identity theft to officially report the crime, enabling them to dispute fraudulent activity with businesses and credit agencies ; it is essentially a legal document that can be used to prove identity theft and is created online through the FTC 's website, with the authority stemming from the " Identity Theft and Assumption Deterrence Act '' which outlines the procedures for reporting identity theft to the FTC. Therefore this company is in violation of my rights per the FCRA, FDCPA, and the Identity Theft and Assumption Deterrence Act. The Fair Credit Reporting Act, 15 U.S.C. 1681 et seq., is federal legislation enacted to promote the accuracy, fairness, and privacy of consumer information contained in the files of consumer reporting agencies. According to the Fair Credit Reporting Act ( FCRA ), when filing an FTC identity theft report, you have the right to request that credit reporting agencies block fraudulent information on your credit report related to identity theft, and businesses are required to provide you with copies of transaction records related to the fraudulent activity upon receiving a copy of your FTC Identity Theft Report ; essentially allowing you to dispute and remove inaccurate information stemming from identity theft. When a company receives evidence that you are a victim of identity theft, they are legally obligated to remove the fraudulent account from your credit report ; if they refuse, you can file a dispute with the credit bureaus and potentially take legal action under the Fair Credit Reporting Act ( FCRA ).

Thats not real validation. Under FDCPA 809 ( 15 U.S.C. 1692g ( b ) ), a debt collector must provide full verification, like the signed contract, the full itemized accounting, and proof that they have the legal right to collect. They didnt give any of that just generic documents. A lease is not a signed agreement with National Collections, and it doesnt prove that they own the debt. In fact, they didnt show any chain of title or ownership rights at all. These debt buyers often buy large portfolios of accounts in bulk in " pools '' and they dont get full documentation with them. So they dont have real ownership, and theyre not collecting on their own debt. Venue is proper in this judicial district pursuant to 28 U.S.C. 1391 ( b ) because Defendant ( s ) conduct business within this district, and the events or omissions giving rise to the claims occurred in this district. Congressional findings and statement of purpose ( a ) Accuracy and fairness of credit reporting ( 1 ) The Congress makes the following findings : ( A ) The banking system is dependent upon fair and accurate credit reporting. Inaccurate credit reports directly impair the efficiency of the banking system, and unfair credit reporting methods undermine the public confidence which is essential to the continued functioning of the banking system. ( B ) An elaborate mechanism has been developed for investigating and evaluating the creditworthiness of consumers and for disseminating credit information to financial institutions and other businesses. ( C ) Consumer reporting agencies have assumed a vital role in assembling and evaluating consumer credit and other information on consumers. ( D ) The consumer reporting agencies have regularly sold consumer reports to various subscribers, including financial institutions, merchants, and other businesses. ( E ) At the same time, the consumer reporting agencies have not maintained a centralized source of information and have not developed uniform reporting standards. ( F ) The lack of uniform standards has resulted in inconsistent evaluation of consumers and has impaired the efficiency of the banking system. ( 2 ) The purposes of this title are ( A ) to require that consumer reporting agencies adopt reasonable procedures for meeting the needs of commerce for consumer credit, personnel, insurance, and other information in a manner which is fair and equitable to the consumer, with regard to the confidentiality, accuracy, relevancy, and proper utilization of such information ; ( B ) to require that consumer reporting agencies maintain a centralized source of information and develop uniform reporting standards ; and ( C ) to regulate the use of consumer reports and to prevent the misuse of consumer reports. ( b ) Definitions For purposes of this title, the following definitions apply : ( 1 ) The term " consumer '' means an individual. ( 2 ) The term " consumer report '' means any written, oral, or other communication of any information by a consumer reporting agency bearing on a consumer 's credit worthiness, credit standing, credit capacity, character, general reputation, personal characteristics, or mode of living which is used or expected to be used or collected in whole or in part for the purpose of serving as a factor in establishing the consumer 's eligibility for ( A ) credit or insurance to be used primarily for personal, family, or household purposes ; ( B ) employment purposes ; or ( C ) any other purpose authorized under section 1681b of this title. ( 3 ) The term " consumer reporting agency '' means any person which, for monetary fees, dues, or on a cooperative nonprofit basis, regularly engages in whole or in part in the practice of assembling or evaluating consumer credit information or other information on consumers for the purpose of furnishing consumer reports to third parties, and which uses any means or facility of interstate commerce for the purpose of preparing or furnishing consumer reports.

- Acknowledge receipt within XXXX business days (12 USC 2605(e)(1)(A))
- Provide substantive response within XXXX business days (12 USC 2605(e)(2))

Under XXXX XXXX XXXX 83 U.S. 271 (1872), "the note and mortgage are inseparable." Without proper transfer of the note, the deed of trust cannot be enforced.

issue: Attempts to collect debt not owed
narrative: I am submitting this complaint regarding the way THD/CBNA ( Home Depot , issued by Citibank North America ) has reported an account on my credit reports as a derogatory account, including charge-off and collection activity, along with a significant history of late payments. I dispute the accuracy, completeness, and verification of this reporting and believe it does not meet reasonable standards for fair and accurate credit reporting. I became aware of the issue after reviewing my credit reports and identifying that THD/CBNA was reporting negative information related to a Home Depot account. This reporting includes a charge-off and, in some instances, separate reporting that suggests both a paid/closed account and a derogatory account associated with the same creditor. The presence of multiple entries with conflicting statuses creates confusion and raises serious concerns about the accuracy of the information being furnished. XXXX of the most troubling aspects of the THD/CBNA reporting is the apparent duplication and inconsistency. My credit reports reflect more than XXXX THD/CBNA entry with different statuses and dates. In some cases, XXXX tradeline reflects a charge-off or collection status with a past-due balance, while another tradeline reflects a closed or paid account with a XXXX balance. Reporting the same creditor relationship in this manner is misleading and gives the appearance of multiple negative events when the underlying obligation, if valid, should be represented clearly and accurately. Additionally, the THD/CBNA account is reported with an extensive history of late payments, including XXXX, XXXX, and XXXX delinquencies. These late payment notations significantly damage my credit profile. However, I have not been provided with complete billing statements, payment histories, or records showing how these late payments were determined. Late payment reporting should be based on documented billing cycles, due dates, and payment application records. Without this documentation, the accuracy of the reported late payments can not be verified. Another major concern is the charge-off designation. The account is reported as charged off with a past-due balance, yet there has been no clear explanation of when the charge-off occurred, what balance was charged off, or how that balance was calculated. A charge-off typically reflects a specific balance at a specific point in time, but the reporting does not clearly identify these details. In some instances, balances appear inconsistent across reports or appear alongside a separate tradeline that shows the account as paid or closed. This inconsistency makes it impossible to determine what the true status of the account is supposed to be. I am also concerned about the lack of documentation supporting THD/CBNAs authority to report this account as derogatory. I have not received copies of any original agreement, application, or contract showing the terms of the Home Depot account. I have not been provided with a complete account history from opening through closure or charge-off. Without these records, I can not confirm that the reporting accurately reflects a valid and enforceable obligation. Furthermore, there is no clear explanation regarding whether the account was ever sold, transferred, or assigned. In some cases, charge-off accounts are later placed with or sold to collection agencies, resulting in additional negative reporting. In my case, the presence of multiple THD/CBNA entries creates uncertainty as to whether the account was internally charged off, externally collected, or otherwise resolved. A fair and accurate credit report should clearly identify the nature of any transfer or assignment, along with the reporting authority of each entity involved. The way this account is reported suggests that automated verification processes may have been used instead of a reasonable, manual investigation. Automated systems often confirm that data exists in a database without confirming that the data is accurate, complete, or supported by original records. Given the conflicting statuses, duplicate tradelines, and lack of documentation, automated verification would be insufficient to resolve these issues. The continued reporting of this THD/CBNA account has caused ongoing harm. The presence of a charge-off, collection status, and numerous late payments negatively affects my credit scores and financial opportunities. It impacts my ability to obtain credit on fair terms and creates an inaccurate picture of my creditworthiness. This harm is especially concerning when the reporting appears unsupported and inconsistent. Another issue is the lack of transparency and communication. I have not received meaningful explanations from THD/CBNA clarifying the basis for the negative reporting, the calculation of balances, or the reason for the conflicting tradelines. Without this information, I can not meaningfully assess or resolve the matter. I am not disputing this account to avoid legitimate obligations. Rather, I am seeking fairness, accuracy, and accountability. Credit reporting has serious consequences, and companies that report negative information have a responsibility to ensure that it is correct, complete, and verifiable. In this case, the reporting by THD/CBNA does not appear to meet those standards. The paper trail for this account appears incomplete. There is no clear, continuous record showing how the account progressed from current to delinquent to charge-off. There is no explanation of how missed payments were identified or how the account transitioned into its current reported status. Without a clear and complete history, the derogatory reporting can not be reasonably verified. I am also concerned about the potential for inflated or misleading impact due to multiple tradelines. Reporting both a charged-off account and a separate closed or paid account from the same creditor can exaggerate the negative impact on a consumers credit profile. A fair and accurate credit report should not double-count negative information or present conflicting narratives about the same account. In reviewing my credit reports, I observed that some THD/CBNA entries show a XXXX balance and paid or closed status, while others show a past-due balance and derogatory status. This contradiction suggests errors in reporting or a failure to properly update or reconcile account information. Such inconsistencies undermine confidence in the accuracy of the reporting. I am requesting that THD/CBNA conduct a full, reasonable reinvestigation of this account. This reinvestigation should include a review of original account agreements, complete billing statements, payment histories, balance calculations, and documentation supporting any charge-off or collection activity. If THD/CBNA can not produce this documentation, the account should be corrected or removed from my credit reports. I am also requesting that any inaccurate late payment entries be deleted if they can not be fully verified with billing records. Late payments should not be reported without clear evidence that payments were due, billed, and missed according to agreed-upon terms. If THD/CBNA believes that the account is accurate and should remain on my credit reports, I request full transparency regarding how that determination was made. This includes identifying what records were reviewed, how accuracy was confirmed, and why the reporting meets reasonable standards. Vague or conclusory responses would not resolve the issues raised. This complaint is submitted in good faith and for the purpose of achieving an accurate credit report. I believe that resolving this issue will require THD/CBNA to either substantiate the reporting with proper documentation or correct the record by deleting inaccurate or unverifiable information. Ultimately, I am seeking a fair outcome in which my credit reports reflect only information that is accurate, complete, and supported by evidence. The current reporting of the THD/CBNA ( Home Depot ) account does not meet that standard. I am requesting CFPB assistance to ensure that this matter is properly reviewed and resolved in compliance with consumer protection laws and fair credit reporting principles.

I am writing to file a complaint against Bank of America for their disproportionate and unfair action of stripping away millions of reward points from my credit card accounts due to a failure to notice their request for confirming my customer data. I have been a customer of Bank of America for approximately 10 years, using both personal and business checking accounts and credit cards. In early XX/XX/year>, while I was vacationing in XXXX, my accounts were frozen due to a legal requirement to confirm my information, such as name and occupation. Although Bank of America sent notifications, I did not see them. When I reviewed my messages, I did find generic text and email messages. In a busy life, a generic message like that can easily go unnoticed, especially if it does not convey the severe consequences, such as permanently closing credit card accounts and losing millions of reward points. There were no prominent alerts or messages within the Bank of America interface. Given the harsh consequences of not confirming my information, I would have expected a prominent pop-up or a clear alert in the messaging area of my profile, explicitly stating that I must confirm the information to avoid my credit card accounts being shut down. There was no clear indication in any correspondence about these severe consequences. Upon returning and verifying my data, my accounts were unfrozen, but all my personal and business credit card accounts were shut down, resulting in the loss of millions of reward points. Despite multiple attempts through calls, branch visits, and discussions with supervisors, I have been informed that these points can not be reinstated. This loss is incredibly frustrating as these points hold substantial value ( I estimate tens of thousands of dollars ). While I understand the legal requirement for the bank to know its customers, the notifications I received were not sufficiently clear or prominent to convey the severe consequences of not updating my information. The data they required confirmation of had not even changed. Generic text messages and emails that blend in with regular correspondence do not effectively communicate the critical nature of this issue. The points accumulated over nearly 10 years are of significant value, and losing them due to inadequate alerts is deeply concerning. Even if Bank of America 's actions are legally justified, the punishment is grossly disproportionate. Stripping away reward points accumulated over nearly a decade because of a missed notification is an extreme measure. It is unreasonable and unfair to penalize a long-term customer so harshly for an oversight. Bank of America argues that they sent correspondence, but my personal information had not changed, and I did not need to update anything. To take away all my reward points and refuse to reinstate them is an excessive and unreasonable punishment. The practice of stripping away reward points accumulated over many years due to insufficient notification is deeply concerning and warrants your attention. I simply don't understand why Bank of America is so insistent. It is as if they used this as an opportunity to remove the credit card points. Otherwise, there is no reason to not return them. It feels like they want to punish me in the harshest possible way. Even branch managers at Bank of America confirmed to me that this is excessive and they have not seen anything like this. Why be insistent on " No, we don't reinstate the points ''? Why? It doesn't make any sense other than they realize the value and consider this a coup. This approach by Bank of America has irreparably damaged my trust in the institution. Their punitive actions without clear and sufficient warning are unreasonable and disproportionate. I urge you to investigate this issue as it represents a significant failure in customer communication and fair treatment. Thank you for your consideration.

narrative: To Whom It May Concern, I am filing a formal complaint against Freedom Mortgage regarding their handling of my loan assumption application. Throughout this process, I have experienced repeated misrepresentation, lack of due professional care, intentional delays, and contradictory statements that have placed me in an extremely difficult position as a consumer. From the very beginning, Freedom Mortgage has provided me with conflicting information about my file status. I was told multiple times that my loan was in underwriting when it was not. Later, I was told my file was conditionally approved, but this was not an official underwriting decision, but merely an email with vague language. These misleading representations caused me to update sellers, incur financial and emotional stress, and make decisions based on false information. In addition, Freedom Mortgage has made numerous errors with my debt-to-income calculations, insurance figures, and treatment of rental income despite having all the documentation from me multiple times. Requests for documents have been duplicated weeks later, suggesting that my file was not reviewed with diligence. Each time I provided exactly what they requested, yet new and contradictory conditions appeared. I escalated the matter several times within Freedom Mortgage, but the lack of accountability and transparency remained. What should have been a straightforward loan assumption process has turned into months of delays, mismanagement, and what feels like intentional stalling. As a consumer, I believe I have been subjected to : Misrepresentation and misleading communication about my loan status. Negligent handling of my file, with repeated mistakes and missing information despite my full compliance. Unreasonable delays that appear intentional and obstructive. Lack of due professional care, creating unnecessary stress and jeopardizing my ability to close on a home. I respectfully request that the CFPB review Freedom Mortgages handling of my file and hold them accountable for these actions. No consumer should have to experience such gross mismanagement when dealing with XXXX of the largest government-backed mortgage servicers. Sincerely, XXXX XXXX

CFPB Consumer Complaint Narrative I am submitting this complaint regarding the servicing and handling of a manufactured-homerelated mortgage transaction by 21st Mortgage Corporation . I owned the underlying land outright and entered into a transaction involving the proposed purchase and installation of a manufactured home on a specific XXXX property. The lender approved and relied upon a retailer, that appeared in its approved retailer system, and proceeded with origination knowing the transaction involved a XXXX property. They should have known whether the retailer, that is XXXX of their approved lenders, was properly licensed. At closing ( XX/XX/XXXX ), a lien was placed on my property for the full amount of the proposed transaction, and that lien remains in place despite the manufactured home never being delivered. After the transaction was initiated, I learned through the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXXXXXX and Insurance that the retailer was not properly licensed in Tennessee at the time of contract ( XX/XX/XXXX ) and closing. The retailer did not obtain licensure until several months later ( XX/XX/XXXX ), after the transaction had already caused harm. The contract specified it would be set up to state codes, but due to lack of XXXX license, did not know state codes. The caused financial harm and no delivery. The lender provided a written interest-only payment document stating that this policy was designed to protect the borrower until the manufactured home was delivered and to prioritize payment related to the home. The manufactured home was never delivered. Despite this, the lender treated the loan as active and booked, added escrow and late fees, applied payments inconsistently with the interest-only document, and took servicing actions as though a completed home purchase had occurred. These actions took place during a disputed transaction where delivery conditions were never met. After written regulatory notice of the licensing issue and dispute, the lender mischaracterized the retailers licensure by referencing current licensure rather than addressing the lack of licensure at the time of contract and closing. The lender also framed the matter as a dispute between the consumer and the retailer while continuing to enforce and service the loan. Credit reporting and servicing activity continued during this disputed and unresolved transaction. I am requesting that the CFPB review whether the lenders conduct constitutes unfair, deceptive, or abusive acts or practices, including reliance on an unlicensed retailer, failure to honor written borrower protections, improper servicing actions, and misleading representations after regulatory notice.

Also with an unknown & inaccurate account number. 3. Eastern Account systems has violated the FDCPA 's prohibition on re-aging or re-reporting deleted debts ( 15 U.S.C. 1692e ). The Fair Debt Collection Practices Act ( FDCPA ) prohibits debt collectors from re-aging or re-reporting deleted debts. This means that once a debt has been deleted from a consumer 's credit report or has reached a certain age, debt collectors are generally not allowed to reset the clock on the debt or re-report it to credit bureaus as if it were a new debt. Section 1692e of the FDCPA specifically addresses false or misleading representations, including reporting inaccurate information. Re-aging or re-reporting a debt that has been deleted from a credit report or has aged beyond the applicable reporting period could be considered deceptive and misleading under this provision of the FDCPA. The prohibition on re-aging or re-reporting deleted debts is intended to prevent debt collectors from unfairly extending the reporting period of a debt or misleading consumers and credit reporting agencies about the status of the debt. This provision aims to ensure that accurate and truthful information is reported regarding the collection of debts and to protect consumers from deceptive debt collection practices. It's important for debt collectors to comply with this provision of the FDCPA to ensure fair and accurate reporting of debts and to protect the rights of consumers. I believe that a debt collector has violated this provision, I may consider seeking legal advice or filing a complaint with regulatory authorities. Failure to provide such documentation will indicate that you are unable to lawfully enforce this alleged debt. Any further collection efforts without proper validation will be viewed as a violation of federal law. 2. UCC 9-208 : Duty of Secured Party Pursuant to UCC 9-208 , if you can not provide verification of a perfected security interest in this debt, you are obligated to release any claim or lien related to it. XXXX. Relevant Legal Precedent Courts have upheld consumers rights to demand thorough debt validation under the FDCPA. In XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX ( XXXX. XXXX XXXX. XXXX ), the court held that a debt collectors failure to validate a debt under 15 U.S.C. 1692g prohibits further collection activities. 4. Cease and Desist Until such time as the alleged debt is fully validated to my satisfaction, you are hereby instructed to cease and desist from all collection efforts, including but not limited to phone calls, letters, credit reporting, or any other form of communication regarding this matter. 5. Remedies for Non-Compliance If you fail to comply with these requirements or continue collection activities without providing adequate validation, I will explore all available legal remedies. These remedies may include filing a complaint with the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau ( CFPB ), my states Attorney General, and/or pursuing legal action for violations of the FDCPA and other applicable laws. Please provide a written response, including all requested documentation, within 30 days of the date of this letter. Failure to respond adequately will result in further action to protect my rights. In the case of any investment made by a savings institution in a real estate loan, if ( i ) the ownership of the real estate security or any part thereof becomes vested in a person other than the party originally executing the security instruments and ( ii ) there is not an agreement in writing to the contrary, a savings institution may, without notice to such party, deal with such successor in interest with reference to that mortgage and the debt thereby secured in the same manner as with such party. I tried numerous times ( unsuccessfully ) to change the bank account details, but always encountered technical or logistical obstacles caused by Flagstars own systems and polices. I attempted to read the instructions on the Flagstar website on multiple occasions, but still despite having worked in the finance / payments industries was utterly befuddled about what I was supposed to do. Compounding the problem, Flagstar also miscalculated the time period that I was " late '' on one of the credit reports ( XXXX ), saying I was " 60 days '' late when " 30 days '' would have been more accurate. Specifically, the XXXX XXXX was due on XXXX, and late fees are not assessed until after the XXXX of the month. By making a double payment for XXXX on the XX/XX/XXXX, this should have been listed as 30-days or ( at most ) 42 days past due. However, the XXXX report says " 60-days late '' which means it was over *2 months* behind, and this is seen as an even worse delinquency by creditors. II. OTHER PEOPLE SEEM TO HAVE HAD THE SAME CONCERNS : In reviewing online CFPB complaints from other persons during that same timeframe ( Spring/Summer XXXX ) I can see that I am not the only one that had these types of problems with your autopay system. In fact, I reviewed many complaints from this past year that contain facts virtually identical to mine, included several submitted to the CFPB. I have included four ( 4 ) examples here with this submission, collectively labeled as Exhibit C. Some of these complainants have theorized that Flagstar deliberately chose to make the autopay process more difficult, in hopes of generating additional late fees as a away of offsetting lower profit margins due to the historically low interest rates in place since the COVID-19 pandemic. I was unable to reasonably avoid the injuries because Flagstar 's act ( s ) or practice ( s ) interfered with my ability to effectively make decisions or to take corrective action. In addition, such act ( s ) or practice ( s ) would not be seen as having an offsetting benefit to consumers. >> Deceptive prong : As mentioned, I received confusing and highly misleading statements ( i.e. instructions ) on the Flagstar website and via telephone support interactions, leading me to believe that autopay on my account was working when in fact it was not. My interpretation would also be considered reasonable under the circumstances, as multiple people in similar situations were complaining about the exact same problems with Flagstar 's autopay system at precisely the same time ( Spring/Summer XXXX ). The misleading statements were " material, '' in that I would not have allowed the XXXX payment to lapse if I had known that autopay was not configured properly. >> Abusive prong : The act ( s ) or practice ( s ) in question were also abusive, in that they materially interfered with my ability to protect my interests in using a consumer financial product or service ( i.e. the mortgage loan autopay service ). See, e.g., https : XXXX XXXX. PayPal Credit engages in deceptive and unfair billing practices related to its 6 Months Interest-Free promotional financing program. While certain purchases qualify for this offer, other purchases accrue interest immediately. The central issue is PayPal Credits payment allocation method. Payments are automatically applied first to the promotional, interest-free balances, and consumers are not given any option to direct payments toward non-promotional balances. This practice prevents consumers from paying down the principal on high-interest balances, ensuring that interest continues to accrue regardless of timely payments. This practice is misleading and harmful because it : 1.Misrepresents repayment control Consumers are led to believe they can manage their debt responsibly, but in fact, they are denied the ability to reduce high-interest balances. 2.Causes unavoidable financial harm Consumers are subjected to compounding interest charges they can not prevent, despite making regular payments. 3.Creates an unfair competitive disadvantage Other creditors generally allow consumers to allocate payments or apply them to higher-interest balances first. Additionally, when I contacted PayPal Credit customer service for clarification, I was advised that I could avoid the issue by making XXXX separate payments. I followed this guidance, paying weekly, yet the result was the same : interest continued to accrue on the non-promotional balance. This demonstrates that PayPals own representatives are providing misleading and ineffective solutions, compounding the consumer harm. This is not an isolated occurrence. In 2015, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau ( CFPB ) took enforcement action against PayPal Credit ( formerly XXXX XXXX Later ) for deceptive practices, including the mishandling of deferred-interest promotions. PayPal was ordered to provide {$15.00} XXXX in redress to consumers and pay a {$10.00} XXXX penalty. Since then, many consumers have continued to report problems with payment allocation under PayPals deferred-interest and promotional financing programs. I believe this practice may violate the following consumer protection laws and regulations : Truth in Lending Act ( TILA ), Regulation Z ( 12 C.F.R. 1026 ) requires creditors to disclose clear terms and apply payments in a manner that is not misleading or unfair. Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act ( 12 U.S.C. 5531 ) prohibits unfair, deceptive, or abusive acts or practices ( UDAAP ). Federal Trade Commission Act ( 15 U.S.C. 45 ) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in commerce.

15 U.S. Code 6801 - Protection of nonpublic personal information U.S. Code ( a ) Privacy obligation policy It is the policy of the Congress that each financial institution has an affirmative and continuing obligation to respect the privacy of its customers and to protect the security and confidentiality of those customers nonpublic personal information. ( b ) Financial institutions safeguards In furtherance of the policy in subsection ( a ), each agency or authority described in section 6805 ( a ) of this title, other than the Bureau of Consumer Financial Protection, shall establish appropriate standards for the financial institutions subject to their jurisdiction relating to administrative, technical, and physical safeguards ( 1 ) to insure the security and confidentiality of customer records and information ; ( 2 ) to protect against any anticipated threats or hazards to the security or integrity of such records ; and ( 3 ) to protect against unauthorized access to or use of such records or information which could result in substantial harm or inconvenience to any customer. 15 U.S. Code 6802 - Obligations with respect to disclosures of personal information U.S. Code ( a ) Notice requirements Except as otherwise provided in this subchapter, a financial institution may not, directly or through any affiliate, disclose to a nonaffiliated third party any nonpublic personal information, unless such financial institution provides or has provided to the consumer a notice that complies with section 6803 of this title. ( b ) Opt out ( 1 ) In general A financial institution may not disclose nonpublic personal information to a nonaffiliated third party unless ( A ) such financial institution clearly and conspicuously discloses to the consumer, in writing or in electronic form or other form permitted by the regulations prescribed under section 6804 of this title, that such information may be disclosed to such third party ; ( B ) the consumer is given the opportunity, before the time that such information is initially disclosed, to direct that such information not be disclosed to such third party ; and ( C ) the consumer is given an explanation of how the consumer can exercise that nondisclosure option. ( 2 ) Exception This subsection shall not prevent a financial institution from providing nonpublic personal information to a nonaffiliated third party to perform services for or functions on behalf of the financial institution, including marketing of the financial institutions own products or services, or financial products or services offered pursuant to joint agreements between two or more financial institutions that comply with the requirements imposed by the regulations prescribed under section 6804 of this title, if the financial institution fully discloses the providing of such information and enters into a contractual agreement with the third party that requires the third party to maintain the confidentiality of such information. ( c ) Limits on reuse of information Except as otherwise provided in this subchapter, a nonaffiliated third party that receives from a financial institution nonpublic personal information under this section shall not, directly or through an affiliate of such receiving third party, disclose such information to any other person that is a nonaffiliated third party of both the financial institution and such receiving third party, unless such disclosure would be lawful if made directly to such other person by the financial institution. ( d ) Limitations on the sharing of account number information for marketing purposes A financial institution shall not disclose, other than to a consumer reporting agency, an account number or similar form of access number or access code for a credit card account, deposit account, or transaction account of a consumer to any nonaffiliated third party for use in telemarketing, direct mail marketing, or other marketing through electronic mail to the consumer. ( e ) General exceptions Subsections ( a ) and ( b ) shall not prohibit the disclosure of nonpublic personal information ( 1 ) as necessary to effect, administer, or enforce a transaction requested or authorized by the consumer, or in connection with ( A ) servicing or processing a financial product or service requested or authorized by the consumer ; ( B ) maintaining or servicing the consumers account with the financial institution, or with another entity as part of a private label credit card program or other extension of credit on behalf of such entity ; or ( C ) a proposed or actual securitization, secondary market sale ( including sales of servicing rights ), or similar transaction related to a transaction of the consumer ; ( 2 ) with the consent or at the direction of the consumer ; ( 3 ) ( A ) to protect the confidentiality or security of the financial institutions records pertaining to the consumer, the service or product, or the transaction therein ; ( B ) to protect against or prevent actual or potential fraud, unauthorized transactions, claims, or other liability ; ( C ) for required institutional risk control, or for resolving customer disputes or inquiries ; ( D ) to persons holding a legal or beneficial interest relating to the consumer ; or ( E ) to persons acting in a fiduciary or representative capacity on behalf of the consumer ; ( 4 ) to provide information to insurance rate advisory organizations, guaranty funds or agencies, applicable rating agencies of the financial institution, persons assessing the institutions compliance with industry standards, and the institutions attorneys, accountants, and auditors ; or to respond to judicial process or government regulatory authorities having jurisdiction over the financial institution for examination, compliance, or other purposes as authorized by law. 15 U.S. Code 6803 - Disclosure of institution privacy policy U.S. Code ( a ) Disclosure required At the time of establishing a customer relationship with a consumer and not less than annually during the continuation of such relationship, a financial institution shall provide a clear and conspicuous disclosure to such consumer, in writing or in electronic form or other form permitted by the regulations prescribed under section 6804 of this title, of such financial institutions policies and practices with respect to ( 1 ) disclosing nonpublic personal information to affiliates and nonaffiliated third parties, consistent with section 6802 of this title, including the categories of information that may be disclosed ; On XX/XX/year>, I went to a local Truist Bank Branch and requested to open a checking & savings account. XXXX Summary of Your Rights Under the Fair Credit Reporting Act.
The federal Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA) promotes the accuracy, fairness, and privacy of information in the fles of consumer reporting agencies.
There are many types of consumer reporting agencies, including credit bureaus and specialty agencies (such as agencies that sell information about
check writing histories, medical records, and rental history records). Here is a summary of your major rights under the FCRA. For more information,
including information about additional rights, go to www.consumer;nance.gov/learnmore or write to: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, XXXX XXXX XXXX Washington, D.C. XXXXYou must be told if information in your ;le has been used against you. Anyone who uses a credit report or another type of consumer report to deny
your application for credit, insurance, or employment or to take another adverse action against you must tell you, and must give you the name,
address, and phone number of the agency that provided the information.
You have the right to know what is in your ;le. You may request and obtain all the information about you in the fles of a consumer reporting agency
(your "fle disclosure"). You will be required to provide proper identifcation, which may include your Social Security number. In many cases, the
disclosure will be free. You are entitled to a free fle disclosure if:
a person has taken adverse action against you because of information in your credit report;
you are the victim of identity theft and place a fraud alert in your fle;
your fle contains inaccurate information as a result of fraud;
you are on public assistance;
you are unemployed but expect to apply for employment within 60 days.
In addition, all consumers are entitled to one free disclosure every 12 months upon request from each nationwide credit bureau and from nationwide
specialty consumer reporting agencies. See www.consumerfnance.gov/learnmore for additional information.
You have the right to ask for a credit score. Credit scores are numerical summaries of your creditworthiness based on information from credit bureaus.
You may request a credit score from consumer reporting agencies that create scores or distribute scores used in residential real property loans, but you
will have to pay for it. In some mortgage transactions, you will receive credit score information for free from the mortgage lender.
You have the right to dispute incomplete or inaccurate information. If you identify information in your fle that is incomplete or inaccurate, and report it
to the consumer reporting agency, the agency must investigate unless your dispute is frivolous. See www.consumerfnance.gov/learnmore for an
explanation of dispute procedures.
Consumer reporting agencies must correct or delete inaccurate, incomplete, or unveri;able information. Inaccurate, incomplete or unverifable
information must be removed or corrected, usually within 30 days. However, a consumer reporting agency may continue to report information it has
verifed as accurate.
Consumer reporting agencies may not report outdated negative information. In most cases, a consumer reporting agency may not report negative
information that is more than seven years old, or bankruptcies that are more than 10 years old.
Access to your ;le is limited. A consumer reporting agency may provide information about you only to people with a valid need usually to consider an
application with a creditor, insurer, employer, landlord, or other business. The FCRA specifes those with a valid need for access.
You must give your consent for reports to be provided to employers. A consumer reporting agency may not give out information about you to your
employer, or a potential employer, without your written consent given to the employer. Written consent generally is not required in the trucking industry.
For more information, go to www.consumerfnance.gov/learnmore.
You may limit "prescreened" offers of credit and insurance you get based on information in your credit report. Unsolicited "prescreened" offers for
credit and insurance must include a toll-free phone number you can call if you choose to remove your name and address from the lists these offers are
based on. You may opt-out with the nationwide credit bureaus at XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXXYou may seek damages from violators. If a consumer reporting agency, or, in some cases, a user of consumer reports or a furnisher of information to a
consumer reporting agency violates the FCRA, you may be able to sue in state or federal court.
Identity theft victims and active duty military personnel have additional rights. For more Information, visit www.consumerfnance.gov/learnmore.
Consumers Have The Right To Obtain A Security Freeze
You have a right to place a 'security freeze' on your credit report, which will prohibit a consumer reporting agency from releasing information in your
credit report without your express authorization. The security freeze is designed to prevent credit, loans, and services from being approved in your name
without your consent. However, you should be aware that using a security freeze to take control over who gets access to the personal and fnancial
information in your credit report may delay, interfere with, or prohibit the timely approval of any subsequent request or application you make regarding a
new loan, credit, mortgage, or any other account involving the extension of credit.
As an alternative to a security freeze, you have the right to place an initial or extended fraud alert on your credit fle at no cost. An initial fraud alert is a
1-year alert that is placed on a consumer's credit fle. Upon seeing a fraud alert display on a consumer's credit fle, a business is required to take steps
to verify the consumer's identity before extending new credit. If you are a victim of identity theft, you are entitled to an extended fraud alert, which is a
fraud alert lasting 7 years.
A security freeze does not apply to a person or entity, or its aUliates, or collection agencies acting on behalf of the person or entity, with which you have
an existing account that requests information in your credit report for the purposes of reviewing or collecting the account. Reviewing the account
includes activities related to account maintenance, monitoring, credit line increases, and account upgrades and enhancements.
States may enforce the FCRA, and many states have their own consumer reporting laws. In some cases, you may have more rights under state law.

FHA has taken the appropriate actions and has determined that lender could not have known about the well and septic prior to closing. No further action is required. It was classified as Tier 4 ( indicating that the Mortgagee did not know and could not have known ). Through two years and nine months of research, recent communication and policy updates from FHA commissioner XXXX XXXX proves that classification was wrong. " According to my team, they have looked into your situation multiple times and have determined that there is nothing HUD can do. They have advised you to file a complaint with your state regulators. While I have asked them to go back to look again, I do not have any reason to believe the answer will be different, and unfortunately another inquiry will likely take at least several weeks at best and possibly longer. Have you filed a complaint with state regulators, the CFPB, the Appraisal Foundation, or anyone else besides HUD? '' Sincerely yours, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX Secretary for Housing and Federal Housing Commissioner U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development XXXX XXXX She also issued the following update to the Defect Taxonomy requiring fraud and misrepresentation be classified as a severity level 1 not 4. Effective Date The provisions of this ML are effective immediately. All updates will be incorporated into a forthcoming update of the HUD Handbook XXXX, FHA Single Family Housing Policy Handbook ( Handbook XXXX ). Affected Programs The provisions of this ML apply to all FHA Title II Single Family mortgage programs. Background The FHA Defect Taxonomy ( Handbook XXXX, Appendix XXXX ) is FHAs quality assurance framework for Title II loan reviews. It provides a consistent method for identifying defects at the loan level, useful data and feedback through structured categorization of defects, and balance between FHAs statutory obligation to mitigate risk to the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX ( XXXX ) and quality assurance business processes. Mortgagee Letter XXXX, Continued 2 The Fraud or Misrepresentation section of the FHA Defect Taxonomy currently states that Findings of fraud or materially misrepresented information can fall into one of two severity tiers : Tier 1 ( indicating that the Mortgagee knew or should have known ), or Tier 4 ( indicating that the Mortgagee did not know and could not have known ). It further states that FHA determines if the Mortgagee knew or should have known based on whether : An employee of the Mortgagee was involved, and/or Red flags in the loan file that should have been questioned by the underwriting Mortgagee. Mortgagees are responsible for the actions of their sponsored TPOs under 24 CFR 202.8 ( a ) ( XXXX ) and XXXX XXXX Section I.A.5.a.v. To better align the Defect Taxonomy with these existing requirements and mitigate risk to the MMIF, FHA is updating the Defect Taxonomy to include fraud or material misrepresentation involving a sponsored TPO as one of the knew or should have known conditions used by FHA to determine whether a Tier 1 severity classification is appropriate. Based on this update, FHA will seek life-of-loan indemnification from Mortgagees when there is evidence of fraud or material misrepresentation involving a sponsored TPO, regardless of whether FHA identifies specific red flags that should have been questioned at underwriting. Please review my initial complaint using the most recent update which requires the lender to mitigate.

In XX/XX/XXXX, I purchased a home in XXXX XXXX XXXX Florida for {$820000.00}. My lender set my escrow based on a projected annual property tax of {$5000.00}. My actual first-year liability is {$14000.00}. My monthly payment has increased by $ XXXXThis was not an error. It was the predictable result of Floridas Save Our Homes assessment cap, which suppresses taxes for long-term homeowners and resets to full market value when a property sells. The formula to project my real tax obligation requires only a purchase price, a county millage rate, and homestead exemption status. It was never run. Had my lender used the accurate post-sale projection, my debt-to-income ratio would have exceeded qualifying limits. I would not have been approved for this loan. I was approved based on a monthly tax figure that bore no relationship to what I would actually owe.A product that calculates this projection accurately has existed since XXXX. It was not ordered at my closing. Nothing required it to be. I understand there is currently no requirement for lenders to use post-sale tax projections at origination. That is precisely the problem. This gap in RESPAs requirements predates Floridas Save Our Homes cap by 21 years and has never been updated to account for it. I am requesting the Bureau use this complaint as part of the evidence base for a rulemaking that would require accurate post-sale tax projections on purchase loans in states with homestead assessment caps. This happens to an estimated XXXX Florida buyers every year. The tool to prevent it exists. The regulation to require it does not.

Finally, I talked my way into speaking with a supervisor named, XXXX, ext XXXX ( or the last number could be an XXXX, my handwriting was poor there ). He was in the XXXX office. XXXX was somehow able to open my file when others said they couldn't. He told me that an old credit card, from a previous account I had with them XXXX years ago, might have been the reason for rejection. He said he had closed that account and advised me to try again. So, I went back to the store, in person, wasted more time, and reapplied. I was rejected a second time! I protested this again but kept being told I'd have to wait for a letter in XXXX to XXXX business days to find out why. A did receive a letter which was written on XX/XX/XXXX. It did give a specific reason for this rejection : " Prior application submitted too recently ''. ( copy enclosed ) I just shook my head, frustrated once again. I continued my saga by again contacting various agents, hoping to find a way I could speak to a human being in the department that issued the credit rejection letter. A partial listing of agents names I spoke to are : XXXX, XXXX, XXXX, XXXX, XXXX, XXXX, XXXX. If i had known how convoluted this organization 's customer service department was, I would have documented everything more carefully. I had still not seen a letter stating why my first application was rejected. I requested another copy be sent to me. On XX/XX/XXXX a letter from XXXX XXXX, a credit bureau XXXX at Synchrony bank ( copy enclosed ) transmitted to me the original letter identifying why I was not approved. The letter said Synchrony bank had " checked a credit bureau and other data sources to verify information on your ( my ) application ''. It went on to say, " ... based on these checks, we are unable to confirm your identity with enough confidence to approve your ( my ) application at this time ''. ( Of course, as stated above, they were able to collect money from me, every month for 29 years for my XXXX 's XXXX card! ) The letter of rejection listed XXXX as the credit reporting agency they contacted ; but, the letter also said that XXXX 's recommendation was not determinant in making the decision to reject my application. Just the same, I contacted XXXX and spoke to XXXX XXXX, a credit agent there. I identified myself sufficiently that he was able to open my file. He said my credit rating was XXXX and that there were no identity issues with my report. He was incredulous that I was not approved for the credit line. I now had, at least, a vague reason why I was rejected. Once again, I talked my way up the ladder and talked to another supervisor who turned out to be in the XXXX. His name was XXXX, badge number : XXXX. I informed him what my letter said and what XXXX had said. He shrugged, showing no empathy for my plight. Smugly, as If I may not be able to comprehend it, he said there are other factors we use to confirm your identity. I asked him what they were. He said I should respond to my letter in writing if I had any further questions. I pressed the matter and said just tell me the 'other factors '. What are they? I said, you're a credit supervisor and you don't know? He suggested again to write the XXXX office referenced on my letter, if I had further questions. I still didn't give up. I was able to speak to a supervisor in the XXXX office named XXXX, badge number : XXXX. I talked to him on XXXX XX/XX/year>. Different from everyone else I had talked to, he thought my credit worthiness was not a factor at all in my rejection. Instead, he thought my application had been rejected because some fraud detection coding in the program kicked it out. I asked, why in the world the word 'fraud ', relating to my identity, did not appear as part of the reason for rejection!! If some form of fraud was detected in information regarding me, I want to know about it!! He replied it 'sort of ' did, when the letter said they couldn't verify my identity adequately. I asked how was I to infer that? He had no answerI At the end, XXXX suggested I might try applying again, since some time had gone by. I wasted more time and did, but was rejected for a third time! I despaired at that point and gave up my own pursuit to find out what happened. I don't need this line of credit. I could simply have gone elsewhere, but this has become a matter of principle to me. I feel I and others, I'm sure, have been victimized by Synchrony 's banks procedures! I am a resourceful person ; but, could not lift the curtain to see what the XXXX XXXX was thinking in rejecting my line of credit. I believe the obstacles are intentional! issue: Applying for a mortgage or refinancing an existing mortgage
narrative: I am filing a complaint against [ Servicer Name ] regarding a wrongful foreclosure on my property at XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXXXXXX, Loan Account No. XXXX. I have multiple loans with this servicer. On XXXX loan, I was already in an active trial repayment plan and making payments. Because of this, when I called to check the status of my loans, I was often given information for the trial repayment loan rather than the loan that was actually facing foreclosure. On Thursday XX/XX/year>, I specifically asked about the loan for this property and was told by a representative that my loan modification was in the final calculation stage with underwriting. I relied on this information and understood that while foreclosure had not been formally postponed, there was still enough time to complete the modification review before the foreclosure auction date. However, because of the XXXX XXXX holiday on XX/XX/XXXX, the bank did not have an extra business day to complete review before the scheduled foreclosure auction on XX/XX/XXXX. The foreclosure sale proceeded anyway, even though my modification was under active review. This constitutes dual tracking, which is prohibited under federal mortgage servicing rules ( 12 CFR 1024.41 ). A servicer may not move forward with a foreclosure while a borrowers complete loss mitigation application is pending. The servicers confusion between my multiple loans, combined with their assurances that underwriting was finalizing my modification, directly misled me about the true status of the foreclosure timeline. I reasonably relied on their statements that my application was being processed and that the review would be completed before the auction date. I am requesting that the CFPB require the servicer to : Provide a full explanation of why foreclosure proceeded while a modification review was ongoing ; Produce all servicing notes, call recordings, and internal communications regarding my applications ; Remedy this wrongful foreclosure, including rescinding the sale if possible. This foreclosure has caused severe harm to me and to the individuals living in the property under an owner-finance agreement, who now face losing their home through no fault of their own.

I am writing in response to your request for information on fees imposed in residential mortgage transactions. With 24 years of experience as a professional certified XXXX XXXX XXXX, I have observed significant industry changes impacting both consumers and XXXX. When I began my career in 2000, XXXX XXXX were received directly from lenders and brokers, with fees paid either by the borrower directly to the XXXX or by the lender/broker after report completion. Challenges in obtaining payment for XXXX were common if a loan did not close, often resulting in financial losses for XXXX. At that time, the typical fee for a full single-family XXXX in my geographic was around XXXX XXXX {$350.00}. The subprime mortgage crisis brought about the Dodd-Frank Act and the establishment of the CFPB which was to protect consumers. While these measures have had positive effects, they have also introduced negative consequences for both consumers and XXXX. Borrowers are now required to cover not only the appraisal cost but also additional fees imposed by lenders for ordering and processing the appraisal, without clear disclosure. Many lenders prohibit appraisers from including invoices or discussing fees with borrowers, leading to misunderstandings and dissatisfaction by the consumer which reflects negatively on the appraiser. For example, a borrower might believe they paid {$800.00} for an appraisal, while the appraiser receives only {$350.00}. The remaining amount is retained by AMCs ( Appraisal Management Companies ) as processing and sometimes there are additional technology fees charged to the appraiser. Attached are redacted examples to illustrate this issue : XXXX. XXXX XXXX XXXX : Pays {$180.00} for a hybrid report plus a {$20.00} technology fee, resulting in a net payment of {$160.00} to the appraiser. The actual borrower fee remains undisclosed. XXXX. XXXX XXXX XXXX : Offers {$330.00} minus a {$12.00} technology fee, netting {$320.00} to the appraiser. The AMC fee is {$240.00}, with the borrower unknowingly most likely paying {$580.00}. XXXX. XXXX XXXX : Offers {$220.00} for an FHA loan appraisal, a fee level unchanged from 2000, failing to meet the " customary and reasonable '' standards required by Dodd-Frank . These examples highlight the disparity between what borrowers pay and what appraisers receive. The current environment incentivizes AMCs to secure appraisals at the lowest possible cost to maximize their portion of the fee. This often results in appraisers being underpaid relative to the professional standards and costs required to maintain licensure, education, and technology in addition to the consumer unknowingly paying a higher fee than what the appraiser receives under the misleading understanding that they are paying that fee for the appraisal. The customary and reasonable fee requirement must reflect actual payments to appraisers rather than the total borrower charge to cover the cost of a vendor for the lender. The current system allows for non-transparent fee structures that disadvantage both consumers and appraisers. I urge the CFPB to address these discrepancies and ensure transparency in fee structures. Implementing fair compensation standards will help sustain the XXXX XXXX and protect consumer interests. Thank you for your attention to this matter.

issue: Credit monitoring or identity theft protection services
narrative: I am requesting the CFPBs assistance in determining whether Capital One continued contacting me or receiving creditrelated information after they reported an account under my personal information as charged off. Despite this, I continued receiving communications from Capital Ones CreditWise service after the reported chargeoff date. These communications appeared to reference changes to my credit information, including alerts related to my XXXX XXXX XXXX credit reports. I am not making any assumptions about Capital Ones actions. I am requesting clarification and documentation so I can understand whether Capital One continued contacting me or receiving creditrelated information after the account was reported as charged off, and if so, what the legal basis was for doing so. Information Requested From Capital One I respectfully request that Capital One answer the following : 1. Did Capital One continue sending emails or alerts to me after the account was reported as charged off? If so, please provide : the dates the times the subject lines and the purpose of each communication I am not requesting the content of the emails only confirmation of whether they were sent. 2. Did Capital One continue receiving creditrelated alerts or data from XXXX XXXX XXXX after the reported chargeoff date? If so, please explain : what information was received why it was received and under what permissible purpose 3. Was Capital One aware that once an account is reported as charged off or sold, the creditor no longer has a permissible purpose to access a consumers credit file? I am requesting confirmation of their understanding of this requirement. 4. If Capital One continued contacting me after the reported chargeoff date, what was the legal basis for doing so? I am requesting a clear explanation of the permissible purpose relied upon. 5. If Capital One did not continue contacting me, then what explains the communications referencing changes to my credit information? I am requesting clarification on how these communications were generated. Why CFPB Assistance Is Needed I can not determine : whether Capital One accessed my credit file whether they received alerts from any credit bureau whether they continued monitoring my credit information whether they had a permissible purpose whether they were aware of the chargeoff status I am requesting the CFPBs assistance in obtaining clear answers and documentation.
